title: Visiting American New Orleans musicians in Paris
summary: She found Armstrong with Bigard commercial and a touring musician worse, Albert Nicholas traditional and good, and says the demanding French public pushed visitors to play purer jazz.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Well, what do you think about the New Orleans musicians who have come there in person? Have you heard Bonnie Bigard, Albert Nicholas, any of those? Yes.

The first time I heard Armstrong with Barnaby Bigard, I was a bit upset because I found that he was making a commercial music. It had a bit of a fabric, a lack of spontaneity. And when I saw Joe Killington when he was in Paris, it was even worse. I thought it was terrible. It was all except jazz. And they were very surprised by the exigence of the French public They thought that the French were more exigent. They thought that the French were more exigent than the American. And when they told them, they were playing the vieux air and they made an effort. Albert Nicholas, I heard him too. It was very good. It was very traditional and very old style. I think they had to tell them that the French public was exigent and they loved things very pure, the jazz very pure. They made an effort and the last musicians who came to come didn't try to make commercial. And in 2013, they tried to play what they wanted to play spontaneously, like they wanted to do it.
